utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Good morning, Mr. President. If I could just introduce one of our legal interns who is joining us this morning. His name is Mladen Trbic. He is working with our case managers and he is from Republika Srpska. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Good morning, Mr. Nikolic. Would you kindly take the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before we go further, could the counsel representing Mr. Nikolic introduce herself, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. LINDSAY
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour. Virginia Lindsay on behalf of Momir Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Your microphone was not on. Could you repeat kindly.

utterances.speaker: MS. LINDSAY
utterances.text: Good morning. Virginia Lindsay on behalf of Momir Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Nicholls, perhaps I need to give Mr. Nikolic a warning pursuant to 90(E).

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: It may be appropriate, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, probably you are aware of this but we have a Rule, Rule 90(E), pursuant to which you may object to answering a question from the Prosecution or the accused or from the judges if you believe that your answer will incriminate you. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I understand that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: However, even if you think your answer will incriminate you and you do not wish to answer that question, the Tribunal has the discretion to oblige you to answer the question, but in such a case, the Tribunal will make it sure that your testimony compelled in such a way shall not be used as evidence in another case, if any, for any offence other than false testimony. Did I make myself understood to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Nikolic. Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I want to first start off just asking a few questions about your background. Could you tell us where you were born.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I was born in Bosnia-Herzegovina, in the eastern part of Bosnia-Herzegovina, in Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And am I right that you grew up in Bratunac and lived there most of your life?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, you're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could you briefly tell the Trial Chamber about your education, basically how far you got in school, the highest degrees you achieved.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I have a degree, a university degree, in political science and also I have a degree in national defence, and I have a degree that enables me to teach in high school. Before that, of course, I completed high school and elementary school.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. And you talked about being able to teach in high school. Could you tell us about your occupation in Bratunac before the war, where you were teaching, what subjects you were teaching.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Before I got my degree in political science and before I arrived in Bratunac, I completed a secondary vocational school in the field of construction. However, I never worked in the field of construction. I went to do my military service. That's what it was called in those days. At that time, people did their military service, and I did that in Slovenia. Fifteen months later, I went to the Faculty of Political Sciences, and I got my degree. My first job was at the Djuro Pucar Stari high school in Bratunac. I taught a subject called national defence and protection.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, just briefly, before we move on, when you lived in Bratunac before the war, did you know a man there named Miroslav Deronjic?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes. I knew Miroslav Deronjic practically all my life. I can put it that way. We were born in the same town, and we're roughly the same age. I think he may be a year older, but I've known Miroslav Deronjic all my life.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And do you have any kind of familial relationship with him?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: We are not related by blood, as we say in our part of the world, however, Miroslav Deronjic married a relative of mine. In the state where I live, and probably anywhere else, he would be considered my brother-in-law on that basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I want to basically briefly go through your military background. Am I right that around 1986 until war broke out, you had a position in the TO in Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: What I heard through the headphones was "sluzenje vojnog roka," doing military service, and that is not what this is about. In 1986, I started working at the staff of Territorial Defence in Bratunac after having worked at this high school. So this is proper employment. This is a regular job within this Territorial Defence Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. That's what I had said, Territorial Defence or TO. And can you just tell us what your position was.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: In the Territorial Defence, I was assistant commander for intelligence affairs -- or, rather, the assistant commander of the staff of TO Bratunac for intelligence affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And were you mobilised around 18 April 1992?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was mobilised, on the 18th of April, 1992, exactly, like many others who had been military conscripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, without getting into it, is it correct that from around the end of May 1992 - excuse me - until November, you were in Belgrade and then you returned to Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes. It is correct that during that period of time I was absent from Bratunac. I was in Belgrade, yes, and then I returned to Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And when you came back in November 1992, did you take a position in the Bratunac Brigade which had been formed by that time?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes. After a while, after I had returned from Belgrade, at the proposal of the brigade commander I was appointed chief of the intelligence and security organ in the 1st Light Infantry Brigade in Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And did you hold that position until the end of the war?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I held that position until the end of the war, until I was demobilised.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, currently you're serving a 20-year prison sentence; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls, before going further, can I know his year of birth.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could you please tell the Judges when you were born, Mr. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I was born on the 20th of February, 1955.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, is it right that in 2003, you pled guilty in this Tribunal to persecutions, a crime against humanity?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And just very briefly, before your plea, when you were meeting with representatives of the OTP, did you at one point claim to have been at Kravica and Sandici and make statements about those crimes which you later acknowledged weren't true and retracted? Could you briefly -- just very briefly explain what happened there.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, I could. It is true that while talking to the representatives of the OTP at one point when the negotiations were well underway, I said precisely that you said just now. The reason I said that is something I'm going to explain to you very briefly. When talking to the OTP, we met a countless number of times, and a countless numbers of times we went back to the same topics, including that one that had to do with Kravica and what happened there. Of course, I understand the efforts made by the OTP, and I understand the methods and work in terms of interviews and endeavours made to get to the truth and the extent of participation of each and every individual, including myself. So the OTP asked me a countless number of times about Kravica, and that many times I said to the OTP that I had nothing to do with Kravica, quite simply that I had not participated in Kravica and that as far as Kravica is concerned, I am only linked by the order that I received from the command of the Drina Corps after the incident that occurred in Kravica; namely, to investigate whether someone from Bratunac Brigade -- or, rather, from the army had taken part in that crime and which structure was it that committed this crime in Kravica. One day, I think it was April, sometime in that period we met up again. The OTP spoke to me again about that, and a bit out of revolt and a bit more -- well, for the reason that I simply didn't know what to do and how to behave. At one point in time I said, "Well, yes. I ordered that. I did that." And immediately after having said that, I realised what I had done. I realised that I had made a mistake, and my lawyers and I stopped these negotiations or talks on that day. One day was a holiday here. It was Queen's Day here in the Netherlands. After that day, I met with the Prosecutor yet again, and together with my lawyer I said to them -- I mean both my lawyers, and I said that I had made a mistake and that in all truth I had nothing to do with that, and I take responsibility for having stated that on the previous day. The Prosecution wanted me to sign a statement, and I accepted that. I said that I had no problem whatsoever. I made a mistake. I'm prepared to sign this statement, and I signed this statement in which I accepted my responsibility for what I had said. In addition to that, there's something in that statement that has to do with a picture. In relation to that, I also wish to explain that a picture had been shown to me. Not knowing anything, absolutely nothing, whether that was me or not, but anyway, the person in this picture really does look like me. So I wasn't sure whether that was me or whether it was somebody else. However, to a large extent, I really do resemble that soldier who is in that picture. And I was in this dilemma until my lawyer investigated the case and until he found the man who is in that picture. Savic is the man. I don't even remember the name any longer. And my lawyer took a statement from him. He took his picture. And, actually, this document, along with his statement and photograph, was handed over to the OTP. That would be it, in the briefest possible terms, in relation to that statement. Every time I testified here, I expressed my regret over the fact that that happened. Once again I'm saying I'm very sorry that that happened. And in all our subsequent contacts, I tried to be totally sincere and to say everything that I know, where I was present, what I saw, and what I investigated as the intelligence organ and what kind of evidence I obtained. That is what I have to say in relation to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. As you spoke about this statement --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could I have 65 ter 21590, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Can you see the document in your language, Mr. Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Is that the statement you were referring to?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is the statement. That is an attachment. This is actually tab B that is part of the overall documents that I signed with the OTP.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: May I tender that, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P4385, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: May I now please have 65 ter 21584. This is Annex A to the joint motion for consideration of plea agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, just briefly, do you recognise this document as the plea agreement which you signed, Mr. Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: First shall we show him the last page?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: We can do that, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I remember. This is the agreement in which I admitted 5(h).

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. And if we could just go to page 4 of the English as well as the B/C/S. We see at paragraph 9, a section: "Co-operation by Momir Nikolic." And now for Mr. Nikolic, if we could just go to the next page, page 5 in the Serbian language.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Do you see paragraph 11, Mr. Nikolic, where it states: "It is understood and agreed by Momir Nikolic and the Prosecution that all information and testimony provided by Mr. Nikolic must be absolutely truthful. This means that Momir Nikolic must neither minimise his own actions nor fabricate someone else's involvement"? Do you remember that part of the agreement, Mr. Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember that, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And you understand your obligation today as stated in that part of the agreement?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course I understand that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: May I tender this document, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. That will be admitted as Exhibit P4386.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, I won't go through it all, but as you said, Mr. Nikolic, since admitting your guilt and entering into this agreement, you've testified numerous times in this Tribunal, most recently in the Tolimir trial last year, as well as in the state court of Bosnia-Herzegovina; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. That's the background finished. I now want to move on to talking about your duties in the security and intelligence organs of the Bratunac Light Infantry Brigade in July 1995. Can you just tell us very briefly how many battalions did that brigade have in 1995?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: The brigade where I was, that is to say, the 1st Light Infantry Brigade, had three infantry battalions as part of it. When I say three infantry battalions, I mean the permanent composition on the basis of the organisational and establishment structure of the Light Infantry Brigade. Of course, every brigade, including my own, can have units attached to it at the same level or at a lower level. However, if you're interested in that, in that critical period, that is to say, in 1995, and before the conflict around the enclave broke out, an Infantry Battalion from the Infantry Brigade in Zvornik was attached to our Infantry Brigade. This battalion was within the establishment of our brigade, that is to say, my brigade, both from the point of view of command and logistics.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, you were, as you said, chief of intelligence and security in the Bratunac Light Infantry Brigade in this period. If you could just explain to the Chamber. Is it typical for one person to wear both those hats, to have both of those duties, or in some other brigades, like the Zvornik Brigade, was the security and intelligence assistant commanders held by different people?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I think your question may have been interpreted inadequately, but I know what you are aiming at. A Light Infantry Brigade is the first level of unit, brigade level, in which -- which has a security organ per establishment. In Light Infantry Brigades, there are chiefs of organs, that is to say, chiefs of intelligence and security organs who have both the intelligence and security role. The two roles are part of the same duty performed by the same person. The first level where you find the two functions separated is an Infantry Brigade as opposed to a Light Infantry Brigade where I was. I was an officer of such a Light Infantry Brigade. As opposed to that, the Bratunac Infantry Brigade had the two posts separately. The chief of organ in a Light Infantry Brigade is not an authorised official as opposed to the chief of security in a Infantry Brigade who is. He has an official ID and a number of powers. In other words, he has the right of search, bringing in people, submitting criminal reports, and other issues from the domain of criminal law, which is something I did not have. In my brigade, criminal legal matters are regulated in a different fashion, and if you are interested how, I may explain.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I will get to that in a minute, Mr. Nikolic. First of all, focusing on intelligence, if you could just briefly for the Trial Chamber explain what -- what your duties are in a few sentences as in the intelligence side of your position.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can. All duties and obligations of an intelligence organ in a brigade are largely defined by a basic rule, although there are more, but this rule is called security --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat the specific name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, interpreters couldn't catch you when you were naming some individuals. Could you repeat your answer, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Maybe, Your Honours, would you mind if I ask him just to begin again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, we got a bit behind on the interpretation. Could you start again and describe your duties as intelligence officer.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I said that the intelligence organ or the chief of the security intelligence organ in terms of intelligence matters is to work based on instructions or a rule which is called intelligence support. In practice in my brigade, as well as any other intelligence officer, worked mainly on the following: An intelligence officer or organ collects, processes, and analyses, as well as forwards intelligence data to commanding personnel so that the commander or the person intended to receive such intelligence information could make timely, purposeful decisions. In shortest possible terms, that is the obligation of intelligence and security organs at the level of brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. And in 1995, in that position in the Bratunac Brigade, was part of what you needed to know about for those purposes you've outlined the situation in the enclave and the situation of the ABiH forces present in the enclave, what they were doing, what movements they were making, and what their plans were?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes. That was the basic task of any intelligence officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. I'll turn now to the security side. Same question. If you could briefly outline for us what that position entailed, what your duties were, and as you started speaking about the issue of criminal reports, you can explain the role of Mr. Zlatan Celanovic in your brigade regarding the security side.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I need to mention a fact for the sake of the Chamber, which is the following: In 1995, I am aware of this fact which is obvious in a number of documents about the separate functions of the security and intelligence organ of the Bratunac Brigade. I don't know the exact date, but this can be verified. In any case, sometime in 1995, in April or May, under the new establishment structure of the Light Infantry Brigade the two functions were separated. However, my situation was specific. The person who was supposed to be chief of intelligence was first at Trnovo in the field, in a completely different theatre of war around Sarajevo. Next, as he had not been trained in intelligence, he had to attend the course before assuming his duties. Theoretically speaking, then at the time my unit did have the two functions separated, but in practical terms nothing changed. I still had both hats on. When it comes to the Light Infantry Brigade, as I said at the beginning, the chief of security and intelligence organ in a Light Infantry Brigade was not an authorised official. That is why [as interpreted] our main task was, in terms of what the chief of intelligence and security in the Light Infantry Brigade is to do in the area of security. In other words, he only dealt with command staff activities. What does it mean? It means that the security organ in a Light Infantry Brigade is to protect his own unit and command from any danger or incursion of sabotage, terrorist, and other groups which may threaten in the first instance the command, then the arsenal, equipment, explosives, et cetera, and the units at their positions. That is command staff security, which is to be performed by the chief of security and intelligence in the Light Infantry Brigade. If we were to split the positions in professional terms as to where in the Light Infantry Brigade the security and intelligence officer is engaged, then I could say that between 75 and 80 per cent of work has to do with intelligence affairs and the rest of the percentage has to do with the Staff Command activities and security matters, which I explained. The primary role of a security organ is that while protecting the unit needs to undertake counter-intelligence assessments based on which -- what does it mean counter-intelligence assessment in the first place? It means that degree of threat is to be assessed either in terms of the command or facilities. Based on that, measures need to be undertaken or proposed to the commander to counter incursions of sabotage and terrorist groups and repel any threat to its -- to the unit's arsenal, personnel and equipment. In my unit the security organ, in addition to counter-intelligence matters, had to collect documents about crimes committed in the area of the unit. This applied to all other units of that level. As regards criminal acts, as I was not an authorised official and could not sign criminal reports, based on the order of my commander a person was appointed who was Zlatan Celanovic. He was a lawyer and had been part of the military police in my brigade. He was engaged in these professional matters such as documenting crimes, drafting criminal reports, and all procedure which was concluded with the signing of a report. Such a report, criminal report, could only be signed by the brigade commander. Zlatan Celanovic prepared all the necessary documents, and the brigade commander then signed all those documents and forwarded them to the military prosecutors, military courts. That is how things functioned more or less in the brigade where I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You spoke about your commander --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: In 1995, who was your direct commander?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: In 1995, my commander was Colonel Vidoje Blagojevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: He would issue orders to you?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes. The commander is the person issuing orders to his officers at the brigade command.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And would you make reports, intelligence reports and other reports, to Commander Blagojevic? Would you report to him?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Of course. It was my obligation, as well as the obligation of any assistant commander. We had to report on what we did and what problems or issues needed tackling.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, if -- what about what I understand is called the so-called professional management or expertise chain? In other words, in the security and intelligence chains, did you report to the Drina Corps assistant commander for security?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course I did. I understand your question, but it is far from being specific. Any professional reporting -- or any reporting is professional reporting, but one can report up the chain of command, and there is the way of reporting along the professional line. Reporting along the command line starts, say, from the level of battalion where the battalion commander reports to the brigade commander, who in turn reports to the corps commander. In terms of professional reporting as regards intelligence and security organs, then the assistant commander in the battalion in charge of security and intelligence reported to me, and then I in turn reported to the Drina Corps intelligence and security organ. This was the reporting along the professional line.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And in July 1995, who were the assistant commanders for security and intelligence at the Drina Corps level?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: In the Drina Corps it was Vujadin Popovic, as far as I know. He was in charge of security affairs, and Lieutenant-Colonel Kosoric was in charge of intelligence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And if you know -- if you could tell us who was in the professional reporting line? Who would Vujadin Popovic report to?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Excuse me. Lieutenant-Colonel Popovic reported along the professional line to the intelligence [as interpreted] administration of the Main Staff headed by Colonel Beara.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: It says "intelligence." Is it intelligence or security headed by Beara?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Colonel Beara was the chief of the security administration. The chief of the intelligence administration was Colonel Salapura.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. It's clear now. All right. I'd like to now, as we continue just talking about how the brigade was structured, just for a little bit talk about the military police. Who was the commander of the military police in the Bratunac Brigade in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: In July 1995, commander of the military police was Mirko Jankovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And I should have asked earlier. What was your rank in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I held the rank of captain in July.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And have you -- well, I'll ask it this way: Who was Mirko Jankovic's direct commander in the military police? Who issued him orders?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: His immediate superior was the brigade commander since Jankovic was the commander of the military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could you tell us if in your position you had any role in giving advice, professional expertise, advice, in terms of the use of the military police?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes. There is an obligation regulated by a rule which is professional management of the military police by the chief and intelligence organ. In that sense, it was my duty and right to issue proposals how to best use the military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. And just to be clear, who would you make those proposals to?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: All proposals that had to do with the use of the military police are presented to the brigade commander. In my case, it was commander Vidoje Blagojevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And then the commander, Blagojevic, could decide whether to accept the proposal, not accept it, or do -- make a completely different order to your proposal?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes. The commander had the discretionary right to accept my proposal in its entirety or in part or to reject the whole proposal and decide to do something completely different. Once he had made a decision, his was the last word. There were no further discussions or proposals made. We began implementing the task as ordered by the commander immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Final question on the military police. Under the framework at the time and the rules, did they have any particular duties in regards to prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes. Orders always had to define the duties of the military police vis-a-vis any POWs, if there are any, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: But generally speaking, were the military police tasked with dealing with captured prisoners?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes. The military police, among other of its tasks, since your question is a hypothetical one, but it was always tasked with providing physical security to POWs. On top of that, the commander could issue different tasks to them if necessary. If you are asking me about their primary role once there are prisoners, it is the task of the military police to secure them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I want to move on to a different topic now and that's about your duties as liaison officer to UNPROFOR and to the various international organisations that operated in the enclaves. What were your duties - let's talk about 1995 now - in relation to DutchBat?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: As regards DutchBat, it was my duty within the area of responsibility of my brigade together with representatives of DutchBat to deal with any issues which may arise due to the violation of the agreement on the demilitarised zones by either of the sides irrespective of who violated the agreement, whether the Muslims or soldiers from my brigade. We dealt with all such issues which cropped up and which presented problems in the day-to-day operation of both of the Dutch and us.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You spoke about issues which may arise due to the violation of the agreement on the demilitarised zone by either of the sides. What types of complaints about DutchBat raise with you about violations on the VRS side?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I can only answer in general terms, because there were many incidents we discussed and tried to solve. In principle, the gravest problem, and I am now talking about the VRS and my brigade specifically, was entries into the enclave. In other words, moving our forces inside the enclave, violating its borders. Then different entries in the enclave by way of sabotage groups. Such occurrences were happening daily -- or regularly. There were also problems with snipers and shooting from the positions of my brigade, i.e., the 1st, 2nd, and 3rd infantry battalions. Then there were also problems which had to do with the entry and departure of convoys and problems of supply of DutchBat in the enclave, specifically during the period between March or April and the fall of Srebrenica. This problem intensified during that time. Those were the main issues we discussed and tried to deal with to the satisfaction of both sides. On the other side --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Let me stop you there and then I'll ask you about the other side in a minute.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You brought up sniping. Did -- speaking now from the Serb side and then we'll talk about sniping from the other side in a minute, from the Muslim side, were you made aware through DutchBat or did you know through your dealings as an intelligence and security officer of whether civilians inside the enclave were wounded or killed from sniper fire originating from the Bratunac Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes. There were irresponsible soldiers who regardless of all the measures taken to prevent such things from happening, they would open up fire, and there were civilians who were killed or wounded, and they should not have been targeted by snipers.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, what were the -- where you started to answer, complaints from your side about sniping and incidents coming from within the enclave? In other words, attacks on Serb positions in violation of the agreement.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Well, the other side in the Srebrenica enclave, well, they didn't demilitarise. Many Muslims, many soldiers, were still bearing arms, and given what the members of my brigade did, well, I could say that the members of the Muslim army did the same things as the members of my brigade. They would kill at the line of separation. They would enter into the depth, lay ambushes. They would kill civilians and others who had nothing to do with the army and were not armed. These people shouldn't have been targeted by snipers. They shouldn't have had ambushes laid for them, and then they also entered areas where we had no actual control, and they would open sniper fire on civilians who were tilling their land and working around their properties. There were also organised attacks, attempts to create better tactical positions in relation to the positions the Serbian side had. So these were the same sort of violations that were made on both sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And just to be clear, those incidents, those violations you're talking about from the ABiH, or Muslim side, those occurred from the time you were appointed to your position in 1992 through July 1995; correct? The whole time?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Well, no. You asked me about a specific period from, roughly speaking - this is how I understood your question at least - from the time when Srebrenica was declared a demilitarised zone. You asked me about that period. During that period of time, the UNPROFOR UN forces were present. It wasn't before their entry before the 18th of April, 1993. We couldn't speak about those things at that time because I didn't have an interlocutor, so we dealt with those issues when DutchBat and the UN forces entered the area and protected Srebrenica as a -- as it was to be protected.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I understand. Sorry, my question wasn't clear. My point was, just quickly, attacks from within the enclave which you've discussed, those occurred before it was declared a safe area as well; correct? And also after it was declared as a safe area against Serb positions and people.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I've been referring to that period, to the period when Srebrenica was declared a demilitarised zone, and I also spoke about the problems that I discussed with the Dutch during that period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, turning to the international organisations in the enclave that you were liaisoned with, can you tell us which organisations were present that you had contact with?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: The orders from the corps commander and -- well, I appointed him for the liaison officer for all international organisations and for all UNPROFOR forces that were in Srebrenica. So I had contact mostly with the representatives of DutchBat, and I think that the Canadians were there before, so I also had contact with UNPROFOR representatives in Srebrenica. The UNHCR had a representative office. Then there was an office of the ICRC. There were representatives from Doctors Without Borders, and I think there were permanent -- there were no permanent representatives of other organisations. Other organisations didn't have permanent representatives there, but there were other visits that were made to Srebrenica, and when they entered the area, I would have contact with them. But the bodies I mentioned were permanently present in the Srebrenica enclave, and they had their own representatives there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Well, briefly, when you met with UNHCR, with ICRC, with Doctors Without Borders, can you just tell us what topics you discussed? We can start with Doctors Without Borders, the last one I mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Well, with Doctors Without Borders, the issues discussed were mostly to do with things that they were interested in. For example, the situation in the territory where I was, where I lived, the situation amongst the population, the health situation, the lack of medical supplies, and had to do with these medical issues. There were also issues that concerned the enclave. They would inform about the situation in the enclave, about the problems encountered by medical personnel in the clinic in Srebrenica. And on the whole, they would speak to me about the situation in health care institutes and about the limited means they had of taking measures, performing surgical operations, and so on and so forth. So what I was mainly involved in was attempts to request of them certain assistance. We had a similar situation in Bratunac. We asked them to help us by providing us with medical supplies, bandages, injections, and so on and so forth. Medical supplies.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And what about the other two organisations you mentioned. Can you just briefly tell us what the talks were, what your contacts with them were about?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: The ICRC on the whole tried -- or, rather, didn't try but was involved in issues that concerned those who had been captured, refugees, people moving from one side to the other. What I particularly discussed with them, and these things I insisted on, was the question of Serbs who remained in the enclave. There were several families who had remained there, so we tried to reach an agreement so that those who wanted to leave the Srebrenica enclave could do so, and they were at our disposal when it came to organising this. We even had meetings at the Yellow Bridge that were organised. They would bring an old woman who had a family, a son, and they lived in Srebrenica. They brought her there so that we could discuss the matter and see whether she wanted to leave Srebrenica or not. We also had other discussions with the ICRC, and ICRC often had certain requests for evacuations of certain wounded or sick people to Tuzla, patients in hospitals. And on the whole, they acted as mediators when it came to submitting requests of the Drina Corps command and the Main Staff. They would do this through me, through the Bratunac Brigade. They would make such requests through us for the evacuation of these people to Tuzla and to other towns that were under the control of the Muslim army. There is one other organisation. The military observers. I also discussed matters them and our discussions mostly had to do with military issues. The delicate issues that I discussed with DutchBat, well, in 99 per cent of the cases, the military observers and myself discussed these very same issues. They wanted to remain neutral in respect of both sides, so we tried to view the situation -- or they tried to view the situation in a neutral manner. They didn't want to be biased, and that is the sense in which we attempted to deal with these military issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. And I'll talk about that a little bit later, some of your other contacts with DutchBat and some of the problems. I want to talk to you now a little bit about the goals, as you understood it, of the VRS towards the Muslim population in Srebrenica going back now to before July 1995. Who was the commander of the Bratunac Brigade before Vidoje Blagojevic?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: The commander of the Bratunac Brigade before Blagojevic was Lieutenant-Colonel Slavko Bijelic [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: We have "Bijelic" in the transcript. Is it Ognjenovic?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes. Slavko Ognjenovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to bring up a document you've seen before, P4075. This is a 1st Bratunac Brigade document from 4th of July, 1994. 4th of July, 1994, not 1995. Report for the brigade member submitted and this one is to the unit, the 3rd Infantry Battalion. And we'll see when we get to the last page - we don't need to go there now - but it's signed by Commander Slavko Ognjenovic. You've seen this document before. Is that right, Mr. Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have seen this document before. I know what it's about.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Before the break, let's start going through this. Paragraph 1 refers to the recent visit to the corps command, the commander of the VRS GS Main Staff, and an indication that he would soon visit some of the corps units, including the Bratunac Brigade. Very simply, that's a reference to General Mladic; correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: The commander of the Main Staff at this period of time was Ratko Mladic. Colonel-General Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Next the commander writes, regarding this document: "This piece of information binds all units and brigade members to carry out all preparations in commands and units regarding combat readiness and to place it at the level that the Bratunac Brigade," it should say, "our Bratunac Brigade is renowned for." What does that mean, just briefly, get everything -- bring things to the level of combat readiness. Could you explain that term?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Let me just be certain about one thing. Let me just check something.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Take your time.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Obviously, this is the intention of the commander of the Main Staff to visit certain units, Drina Corps units, amongst other units, and Bratunac Brigade units or the Bratunac Brigade. Whenever there was a visit by the commander -- commander from the high command, a corps commander, or commander from the Main Staff, in fact, any such visit would mean that the commander would control certain things. Well, he'd go to a unit, see what the situation was like in a given unit. He would visit certain positions, see how the units had been fortified, how they had dug in, what the situation was with regards to trenches and places to defend oneself from artillery fire. So the combat level of units was at stake. The commander would visit these units to check the situation in the unit and to ensure that the unit was at the level that the unit of -- in question should -- should be at. When we speak about combat readiness, this means that with regard to all aspects of combat readiness, all matters should be dealt with. So the first paragraph, in fact, means that the brigade or the soldiers should be at their positions. They should be equipped, militarily trained. They should be armed. They should have a sufficient amount of ammunition, all other military equipment that is needed for combat. So this is full combat readiness for the units that are to be visited by the commander of the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls, if it is convenient.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, that's fine, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We will take a break for 20 minutes and resume at 10.40.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Continuing with this document on the screen, I'd like to go down to the bottom of page 2 in the English. And we need to scroll down a little bit in the B/C/S as well. Actually, to the next page in the Serbian. Now, there's a part, that political situation at the beginning of paragraph 2 which I won't go into now, but I want to read this part to you at the bottom of page 2 in English: "We have won the war in the Podrinje, but we have not beaten the Muslims," can we turn the page of the English, "completely which is what we must do in the next period. We must attain our final goal, an entirely Serbian Podrinje. The enclaves of Srebrenica, Zepa, and Gorazde must be defeated militarily. "We must continue to arm, train, discipline and prepare the RS army for the execution of this crucial task - the expulsion of the Muslims from the Srebrenica enclave. "There will be no retreat when it comes to the Srebrenica enclave. We must advance. The enemy's life has to be made unbearable and their temporary stay in the enclave impossible so that they leave the enclave en masse as soon as possible, realising that they cannot survive there." Now, from being there as a member of the Bratunac Brigade at the time this document was issued, and we will see later it was disseminated throughout the units, what's the message? What is the goal that is being telegraphed to the brigade in this document from the commander?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: What you have just read out, I could say the following about it: There is a part here that concerns the soldiers, the enemy, and in my opinion there's nothing questionable about that part. It could have been drafted differently with the same objective. It would have the same objective from the military point of view, make the enemy's life impossible, make survival in the enclave impossible. All that's military objective, and there's nothing questionable about that. Nor is there anything questionable about the measures that should have been taken in order to defeat the enemy. What is questionable, however, is the following part, where it says that the conditions should be made unbearable so that the enclave is left en masse. I -- if I didn't know what had happened, then this would just be a political assessment, in my opinion, or a political position, but since I do know what happened in 1995, this can then be placed in the context of that year, the year of 1995, when, in fact, the entire Muslim population did leave the enclave and the enclave was emptied. After we read this document, this is the first thing that occurs to me. That's the essence of what is stated in these two paragraphs that I have just had a look at.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Let's look at the last paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Next page of the English. Two pages on. To the last page of the document. If we can do the same in the Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: It states: "Circulate this report among all brigade members and have them sign for it. Review the report in companies. Morale assistants are to introduce it in battalions, while the assistant for morale, religious and legal affairs is charged with introducing it in the brigade command and staff units. At the same time he will be held responsible for accurate interpretation of this report at the brigade level." Now, did that in fact happen? Was this document circulated as ordered?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes. This document, this information, in fact, was implemented in its entirety. The order was carried out, the order issued by Commander Ognjenovic, and he stated the manner in which the order was to be carried out in the brigade units and at the level of the brigade command.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now I want to ask you what the effect of this order was. You started talking about it. In your previous testimony you referred to it as giving the green light. What did this give the green light to, to the members of the Bratunac Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I know exactly what happened and how this information was disseminated amongst the troops and the members of my brigade. If the Chamber is interested in this, I can provide you with a detailed explanation, but the result of this information, as far as I know, in my opinion, in fact it's not just my opinion, this was borne out by subsequent events, but this information legitimised lack of discipline at the lines of separation, and the soldiers having been provided with this information acted in a certain way. What DutchBat and myself spoke about with regard to the violation of borders, about snipers, about infiltration, about targeting civilian targets - I'm talking about the members of my brigade now - but everything that we tried to prevent and to reduce to a minimum, after this information was disseminated action was stepped up. Sniper action was stepped up. There were several attempts to enter the depth of the enclave, and there was absolutely no necessity to do this, no need to do this. As far as tactical positions are concerned, the other position obtained or reached wasn't any better than the previous one. But quite simply stated, the truce was violated, the borders of the enclave were violated, all the things that we spoke about, all the things that we tried to find a solution to failed. But I am limiting myself to the zone of responsibility of the Bratunac Brigade when I make this claim. For the benefit of the Chamber I would like to add that I wasn't responsible for the incidents throughout the enclave in Srebrenica because there were neighbouring units that were also present. I'm only responsible for the zone of responsibility of my Bratunac Brigade. I want this to remain very clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. We talked about sniping a little while ago and you talked about it now so -- and said that sniper action was stepped up. Again, aside from soldiers who may have been shot by snipers from the Bratunac Brigade, what -- can you describe what the circumstances were in which civilians would be shot from the Bratunac Brigade after this information was distributed to every member of the brigade? Just explain what types of incidents were brought to your attention. What were these people doing, some of whom were wounded or killed?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: With regard to sniper fire from the positions of the units in my brigade, all I can say here is that sniper fire was opened from the positions of all battalions, from the positions of the Zvornik battalion, which was within my brigade, from the positions of the 1st, 2nd, and 3rd Infantry Battalion as well. I most frequently had to intervene and visit the positions myself because of the situation in the 2nd Infantry Battalion, which is in immediate contact -- well, was in immediate contact with the Likari village, the Budak village, the Potocari village, and the villages in front of the forward edge of the 2nd Infantry Battalion of my brigade. Who were the targets? I as a soldier, as an officer, believe that an armed soldier is a legitimate target. If he is preparing to attack you or is moving around with weapons and is provoking you, these are legitimate targets in my opinion. Members of the DutchBat and myself never organised meetings if it was a matter of soldiers who were opening fire on each other and wounding each other. This is something I believed to be -- well, not normal. There shouldn't have been any shooting, but it was war, and we believed that it was not possible to prevent such things. As for the targets of snipers, they were most frequently civilians in front of the forward position of the 2nd Infantry Battalion in the village of Dugo Polje, in Likari village. There were people who were tilling their land, working their fields, sowing. They were working on their houses and their gardens and so on and so forth. So these civilians were then targeted by snipers, and on such occasions, the DutchBat representatives would complain. They would come to see me. We would organise meetings and we would try to deal with these issues. That's what I can say in brief about it. And naturally in other battalions, too. I received information that sniper fire was opened in Buljim. Then there was the Zvornik battalion area, the 1st Infantry Battalion in the Vresinje area. That was also an area towards Bijeceva [phoen] where sniper fire would be opened. From the 2nd Infantry Battalion there is a position called Zvijezda, and they'd open fire in the direction of the villages I have mentioned. In the Zalazje sector, in the Pribici [phoen] sector sniper fire would also be opened. But it was in the zone of responsibility of the 2nd Infantry Battalion that such activity was most intense, as I have already said.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I do apologise, because I held my hand up.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: It's okay. Could I move on now to 65 ter 03655, please. This is a Drina Corps command document signed by the corps commander Zivanovic, dated 24 July 1995 [sic]. Defining tasks from the briefing and urging their completion. If we look at the paragraph just above "Order." This is now 20 days after the document we just looked at. We see that pursuant to a briefing on 01 July 1994 to the VRS Main Staff commander by Drina Corps commander and regiment brigade commanders about the level of combat readiness in units and corps commands, and it continues, the following order is being issued to regulate measures, actions and tasks relating to the Muslim enclaves at Srebrenica, Zepa, and Gorazde. You recall you've seen this document before, Mr. Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, I saw this document before, but I think that you misspoke. It's the 24th and 22nd of July, 1994, whereas you said "1995" and that's what the transcript says, so I think that should be corrected.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. It's 24th of July, 1994, talking about a visit on the 1st of July briefing, 1994. I just want to look at a couple sections.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: If we could go to paragraph 3 in both versions. If we can scroll over on the Serbian. I don't think the witness can see the entire page. Scroll it to the left. If we scroll over we can see the paragraph numbers, hopefully. All right. Well, I'll read it out.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Paragraph 3 begins: "No equipment is to be allowed into the 'enclaves,' apart from food and medication which are approved by the VRS Main Staff." Can you see that in your section, sir?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: If we could now go down in the English version and to page 2 on the Serbian. We see: "All authorised cargo and people (authorisation from the VRS Main Staff) is to be thoroughly checked at the following check-points." And below that: "When leaving the enclaves, from the enclaves of Srebrenica, Yellow Bridge" -- "Yellow Brigade," it says, "responsible command 1st Bratunac Light Infantry Brigade." And if we can go on now to page 4 of the English. Paragraph 9. Which is page 3 of the Serbian. We see: "The commands," in paragraph 9, "of the 1st Bratunac Light Infantry Brigade, the 1st Zvornik Light Infantry Brigade, Pribicevac Tactical Group, Skelani Independent Infantry Battalion, the 1st, 2nd and 5th PLBRs that hold the position around the 'enclaves' are obliged to engage in the 3rd level fortification and complete mining along the lines reached. Therefore, at the front end a connecting trench is to be dug, but where that is not possible, a stone wall is to be built or wooden fence - so the enclave would be completely surrounded, that is, fenced, and so it would be made impossible for the Muslims to leave the enclave." So the sections I've read out discuss no equipment is to be allowed into the enclaves apart from food and medicine approved by Main Staff. All authorised cargo and people again are to be checked on authorisation from the Main Staff, and there is this reference to preventing anybody from leaving, Muslims from leaving the enclave. Can you just tell us what this order is about? What is this order?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic. On what are you objecting?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm afraid it is a language issue again. The interpretation I heard a moment ago was that they were leaving the enclave and now it says abandoned the enclave. They were leaving the enclave in a combat sense. There are major language problems involved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I can't follow the B/C/S, but now Mr. Nikolic should have heard your intervention, and having read the -- this order, I think we can proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: My question was: What is this order about? What is this order stating about control of items going in and out of the enclave and control of movement of Muslims out of the enclave?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: This specific order is what you read out, basically, but on the whole, it relates to an order that has to do with the checking of cargo, persons, everybody and everything entering the enclave and leaving the enclave. That is defined in one of these items. Also what is defined are the directions of entering the enclave and the direction in which convoys leave the enclave. What is important for me and what I know is the direction in which convoys moved into Srebrenica and out of Srebrenica, down a macadam road along the Drina River, and that was the route that had been assigned for convoys. This order also defines who carries out the main checks, full control. That is to say, all convoys leaving entering Srebrenica are checked in detail on the Yellow Bridge, whereas all of those entering Srebrenica and are coming from Serbia are being checked in the area of Karakaj, in the area of responsibility of the Zvornik Brigade. Also in this paragraph number 9, yes, yes, item 9, regulates measures that have to do with preventing departures from the enclave, if I understand this correctly. For the benefit of Their Honours, I would like to say the following, what Mr. Karadzic intervened a moment ago -- actually, there are two ways in which departures could be carried out. That is to say, those who went out for diversions, sabotage, incursions, and that is the armed Muslims who were leaving the enclave. And then there is this other kind of departures, Muslims who, through the combat positions of my unit and other unit, primarily in the direction of Kladanj and Tuzla, basically through the battle order of the Milici Brigade, they were leaving illegally and going to Kladanj and Tuzla. That's the way it was. These are civilians. I'm talking about civilians who were leaving for a variety of reasons. And they were going out. Sometimes they managed to cross all of these lines and leave safely. Sometimes they did not manage to do so. Sometimes they'd get into minefields and fall victim there. So I'm just trying to make addition continuation between those military departures from the enclave and, on the other hand, these civilians, these civilians who individually or in groups left the enclave.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter notes: Could the witness please be asked to speak slower. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Also in paragraph 9 this has been defined, the closing of the enclave, but the order itself regulates that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, the document we saw before this, signed by Commander Ognjenovic, and you commented that you didn't agree with it, it said that the -- that life must be made unbearable so that the people in the enclave would realise that they could not survive there. This document talks about setting up walls or preventing people from leaving. So what, in your understanding, was the goal of the VRS towards the Muslim population of the Srebrenica enclave at this time? Did they want them to all stay there or did they want them to all leave?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Well, I cannot speak on behalf of others what it was that they were thinking. I can give you my own position, my own line of thought with regard to this question, and that is what I'm going to tell you here. I personally thought along the following lines. If families or civilians are leaving Srebrenica or if they have to leave Srebrenica, then the soldiers who remain -- actually, in my view, then there is no more any motive to organise defence or engage in combat or have any kind of armed resistance. Certainly. I say certainly. Well, actually, now I can speak a bit on behalf of these people where I was born and where I live. Everybody who lived there, in view of everything that had happened until then, wanted to have the enclave of Srebrenica emptied. They wanted them to be defeated militarily, and they wanted it to be emptied as an enclave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls, let me clarify this. Mr. Nikolic, a moment ago you said that the civilians, Muslim civilians were leaving illegally and going to Kladanj and Tuzla, referring to two kinds of departure from the enclave. Did you mean by saying "leaving illegally," that Bosnian authorities prohibited their own citizens from leaving the enclave? What did you mean by "illegally"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is what I meant: In addition to these departures that Mr. Nicholson [sic] asked me about, there were legal departures as well from the enclave. There were organised convoys, in 1994, if I remember correctly. There were organised convoys when - and this is my free estimate - between 3.500 and 4.000 Muslim civilians left. So these are legal departures of Muslim civilians from the enclave along with proper permission and at their own request, and then the authorities in Srebrenica forbade legal departures, and once they forbade these legal convoys towards Tuzla and free territory, then certain families and civilians left illegally. They tried to make do. They tried to get to Tuzla, Olovo, Kladanj, this free territory. That is what I meant when I said "illegal departures." As for military departures, this was regular practice. This is combat, ambushes, incursions, sabotage, involving that kind of departure from the enclave. That is a military thing. Whoever leaves or enters in that way takes upon himself the risk of doing that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Nikolic. It is Mr. Nicholls that is asking you questions now. Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Let me move on, Mr. Nikolic, now to the movement of convoys in and out of the Srebrenica enclave. I'm speaking -- I'm going to speak about convoys to resupply DutchBat, we'll talk about 1995 now, as well as humanitarian aid convoys; all right?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Can you first tell us, briefly as you can, but give us an overview of how this worked. When convoys came to enter, tell us about the authorisation process and which bodies gave the authorisations regarding convoys and the equipment which could come in or out as you experienced it as security and intel chief. I understand these were passed down to your brigade from above.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I'll try to answer as briefly as possible. Any convoy that was supposed to enter Srebrenica, regardless whether it was a convoy for meeting the needs of DutchBat or whether it was a UNHCR convoy or whether it had to do with any other convoy that would enter Srebrenica, this is how things happened. At the level of Republika Srpska there was this so-called co-ordination body. This co-ordination body, well, basically I even know what their composition was. Part of these people who worked in the co-ordination body were from the civilian structures, the civilian authorities, but there were also representatives of the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska. As regards every convoy that was supposed to enter, they would issue their own approval, and that would define everything very specifically. The number of trucks, the content of the convoy, the number of persons -- or, rather, soldiers, along with their IDs, and everything else on the basis of which you could see exactly who it was that was supposed to enter Srebrenica. In most cases, my brigade would receive these approvals down the chain of command; that is to say, the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska, the command of the Drina Corps, and the Bratunac Brigade. Or if it has to do with an urgent matter, if there is not enough time, then this kind of approval would come directly to the commander of the Bratunac Brigade from the Main Staff. So that was the green light for the convoy to enter Srebrenica. There were cases -- you should know this as well. There were cases when -- I mean, I remember situations like this. The late Vice-President Koljevic sometimes signed on behalf of the co-ordination body, and for us such documents -- or, rather, such approvals had the function of an order. Of course, when it would come from the Main Staff, of course it would be an order, but when this would arrive with the signature of Mr. Koljevic, we would take that as an order that we would fully carry out as written.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. And we'll get to a couple documents in a moment, but what was your -- concretely what was your role in this process when convoys were coming to enter the enclave?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: My role was roughly as follows: In my brigade, in the area of responsibility in my brigade there was a particular point that was called the Yellow Bridge. That was the last check-point before entering Srebrenica or, rather, the territory of the Srebrenica zone. At that check-point -- so it was a check-point. That is where there were members of the military police and also there was a permanent team there that carried out these checks. My role in terms of normal functioning, I mean when there were no limitations or any special orders apart from the regular ones that came in, my role was -- well, how do I put this? It was more one of supervision to bear in mind that the order that had arrived from the Main Staff is fully carried out. And if there is a problem, then I should go there and resolve this problem on the spot depending on the problem involved and the procedure that we would apply.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: P04190, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls, do you tender that previous Drina Corps document?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P4387, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, this document is headed "Main Staff, Army of Republika Srpska," dated 2nd of April, 1995. It's to the commands of the Drina Corps, the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, and Eastern Bosnia Corps. Mr. Nikolic, do you recognise the handwritten portion on the top right?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. What is written in the upper right-hand corner is a text that I wrote and signed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Can you just read it out to us, please. Try to avoid any objections or questions.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Of course. "Not a single convoy or International Committee of the Red Cross team or MFS," I made a mistake there, "may enter Srebrenica without my permission and presence." And then it's signed in my name, Momir Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. And just as an example, if we can go down to paragraph 3. We see these markings on the document in paragraph 3 and a description of this of the 5th of April, 1995, ICRC team trip and the vehicle contents, 50 pencils, five marker pens, ten stapler boxes, four bottles of red ink, five rolls of Sellotape, et cetera. Can you comment on this level of detail in the contents which we see in this Main Staff document?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Of course. Of course I can. As far as I can remember, approvals for convoys to enter, well, let me say in 99 per cent of all cases were this specific and exact quantities would be defined and would then be written in the permit itself. So this order is no different -- I'm sorry, it's an approval actually. This approval does not differ in any way from those received by other organisations and convoys. So this was a kind of blueprint, if you will, informing the check-point of the Yellow Bridge, or, rather, the Bratunac Brigade about the content of the convoy that is supposed to enter.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And if we scroll up a bit now to the top. Go to the top of the Serbian as well, please. It begins: "We hereby inform you that we consent to the request of the RS coordinating body for HP," which for me is translated as "emergency services," "as follows ..." And now if we go to the back page, please, the last page to, see who signed it. And it's signed by General Manojlo Milovanovic, Chief of Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Was it normal or routine that General Milovanovic would sign such documents, to the best you remember? Such approvals?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes. Most of the orders that were sent directly from the Main Staff to the Bratunac Brigade were signed by the Chief of the Main Staff -- or, rather, the Chief of Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska, Mr. Manojlo Milovanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And the coordinating body that we saw on the first page, that's the same coordinating body you were referring to; is that right? The civilian coordinating body?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. That is the body that I referred to a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. Just to be clear, where were these -- I think I understood you, but where were these checks made? Were they made at the Yellow Bridge?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: If you're asking about this date, this time, this period, yes. All checks were carried out at the Yellow Bridge.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, you earlier today talked about in relation to convoys the period in 1995, March, April, May, June. Do you remember you started talking about that?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could you please tell the Trial Chamber during that period what was going on with resupply to DutchBat? What was being approved, and what level of supplies were going in to DutchBat? Fuel, food, that kind of thing.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Their process of resupplying is a complex issue, but I'll try to put it in a few sentences. In this period I mentioned between March and June -- well, April was already the month when the measure restricting the movement of convoys was already imposed, as well as quantities of fuels and lubricants intended for the use of DutchBat in the enclave. My role and the role of the check-point at Yellow Bridge was reinforced, because there were requests by the Main Staff or written orders to strengthen control measures at the Yellow Bridge, irrespective of the fact that the Yellow Bridge was usually the last check-point on]at which something could be controlled on a convoy entering Srebrenica. As far as I know, during that period limitations were imposed on the, first of all, quantities requested by DutchBat, and I speak from experience and about what I discussed with them personally. They frequently put that question, which I then forwarded to the corps command at the Main Staff, with regard to the quantities of fuel they needed. The quantities they received were insufficient for their APCs and vehicles they had at their disposal when implementing their tasks. They also had problems with certain types of food. I need to say here that with regard to that, they also received supplies from -- actually, the Serb side received supplies from the Hotel Fontana from some of the stock used by the Dutch as well. The problem they also had were rotations of soldiers and platoons who were supposed to leave the enclave and were supposed to be replaced by other soldiers. They kept putting that question to me as something that I had to relay to my superior command in order to deal with it. I'll try to be brief. In that period, April, May, June, and July, and until the beginning of the operation, in my view they received inadequate quantities of fuels, lubricants and everything else that was necessary for the functioning of their unit. I knew that at the time, and I knew the exact quantities, but I have forgotten in the meantime. I had access to all documents, and I knew exactly how many soldiers they had, how much fuel, oil, rifles, machine-guns, heavy weapons, et cetera. That was all part of my job as intelligence officer. I knew everything they had, and I could draw my own conclusions as to their combat readiness during that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. You said you'd forgotten in the meantime. Let me see if I can -- if this helps you remember a bit. In your Tolimir testimony at page 12325, you stated: "According to my estimates, not even 10 per cent, speaking of fuel, would enter the enclave. And I'm talking about 10 per cent quantity that I, as a layman, would consider the necessary quantity." So just think about it. How severe was the deprivation of fuel to DutchBat in this period?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Again, I have to be precise. As an intelligence man, I can address such assessments based on the information and knowledge I had. Of course, such assessments need not necessarily be accurate, but at least they were approximations, and I believe they were valid. The quantities that I was familiar with were insufficient for them to implement any tasks. I knew how they worked. I knew their check-point positions, and I knew how they controlled the area and used their APCs and all the vehicles they needed to be able to control the protected area of Srebrenica. I don't think I was mistaken if I said that they received minimum quantities. In my assessment, they received minimum quantities needed to carry out all tasks they had in that period as of the moment such restrictions were imposed. I think they received minimum quantities which were insufficient. As a soldier, I claim that their combat readiness and ability to implement tasks was reduced to a minimum and was insufficient, given this problem with fuel and all other problems. I don't think they were capable of executing combat or other purpose tasks they had in the enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I want to ask you now about supplies, humanitarian supplies, during this period. How much, from your knowledge as intel and security officer, how much of the necessary humanitarian materials, food, clothing, et cetera, was reaching the enclave during this period?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Humanitarian goods that were supposed to arrive by way of UNHCR convoys was coming in -- were coming in. There were several types such as flour, oil, salt, sugar, canned food, et cetera. Those were mainly the items that were arriving. I never analysed that segment in detail as to its sufficiency compared to the number of people in Srebrenica. The number of people were also my assessment, of course. The convoys did go through. Sometimes there were requests to halve the quantities that such convoys carried, but I can't address any specific quantities and whether they were sufficient for the enclave. In any case, there were frequent requests that the convoys organised by the UNHCR be halved as well, or that a quantity of this be allowed and a quantity of that be not allowed, or there were requests that some of it be left to the Serbs. The Serb side believed that they were -- the other side was receiving too much as compared to the Serbs, but I'm no longer in position to discuss whether that was enough or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
