utterances.text: All right. Well, in your prior testimony in the Tolimir case, you discussed the living conditions in the enclave for the people who lived there before the fall, and you describe what your understanding was, your knowledge of what life was like for the people who lived there. Can you please tell the Trial Chamber what it was like, as far as you knew, for the people, the civilian population living in Srebrenica leading up to July 1995?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes. It is correct that I discussed life there based, of course, on my knowledge. What I am about to say mainly includes information received from the people who, as I said last time -- well, there were people who were fleeing the enclave, entire families who fled to the [Realtime transcript read in error "west"] Serb side and they simply wanted to leave Srebrenica. In discussions with them, as well as through some other channels, my information was, as regards the civilians in Srebrenica, that the situation was very bad, that civilians, entire families, literally had no bread to eat or any other food and that they lived on what they could harvest from whatever they managed to plant there. Also, the health situation was bad. There were many sick civilians who could not be in receipt of medical assistance, et cetera. In the enclave as regards the civilians, the situation was quite grave. For certain families, it was even hopeless. They had a terrible life in the enclaves.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] An intervention on lines 13 and 14. It seems that entire families and soldiers fled to the west whereas the witness said the Serb side. It was inappropriately recorded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. When you would like to intervene, please wait till the interpretation is completed. Please do not overlap. Thank you. Yes. Let's continue, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Nikolic. I'm going to move ahead now and talk about what's called either the fall or liberation of Srebrenica in July --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Nicholls, if you leave the topic of convoys, can I intervene here. Mr. Nikolic, we heard from you about the resupply of UNPROFOR as well as humanitarian convoys. From that, I take it there were two kinds of convoy, i.e., humanitarian convoy such as for UNHCR, ICRC, or MSF on the one side, and the convoys for UNPROFOR on the other side. Am I correct in so understanding?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Your understanding is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Were the procedures for those two convoys identical or there were different rules for the two -- two convoys respectively?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Technically speaking, they were exactly the same, starting with permissions being granted and ending with Yellow Bridge check-point controls. Notifications and approvals did not differ for any kind of entry into the enclave. The procedure was identical.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Were the organs dealing with those different convoys the same one? More specifically, did the co-ordination body headed by Vice-President Koljevic also deal with UNPROFOR military convoys?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know about that level. I don't know whether there was any difference, the way the coordinating body treated them and whether someone was specifically tasked with this or that type of convoy. What I know with certainty is that permits were sent to us, the soldiers from the Main Staff of the VRS. Perhaps at the coordinating level there were differences in terms of those convoys aimed at the Dutch and -- as opposed to the UNHCR. I know that Mr. Kekic was in charge of UNHCR matters, but there's nothing I can tell you about that level of decision-making, and I don't know what their relations were. In terms of my brigade, we received orders through military channels, and that is what I know as a -- for a fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Nikolic. Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now I want to talk to you about, as I said, the period of the beginning of the attack on Srebrenica on July 6 and the period up until the fall or liberation of the enclave. Do you recall in the days preceding the fall of the enclave any Drina Corps officers in Bratunac coming to the command?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: You were asking me about the period on the eve of the attack before the 6th of July, just before the attack?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm not constricting it so much. If you can tell us around that period, 6, 7, 8 July, if you saw officers of the Drina Corps and when. For example, did you see General Zivanovic, General Krstic, and, if so, when did you see them in Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Of course, in that period just before the attack, as well as during the attack, I saw a number of officers whom you mentioned, specifically General Krstic, and I mean the corps command. So General Krstic, General Zivanovic, Lieutenant-Colonel Popovic, Lieutenant-Colonel Kosoric. I saw at that time, around the 8th, also General Mladic and Colonel Jankovic from the Main Staff and so on and forth. I saw commanders of assault groups who were all from the units of the Drina Corps. I saw many officers during that period at the Bratunac Brigade command, because many of them came there as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. And you mentioned Colonel Jankovic from the Main Staff. Can you tell us his first name?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Radislav Jankovic, a colonel of the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And what was his position in the Main Staff or which -- which organ did he work in?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Colonel Jankovic worked in the intelligence administration of the VRS Main Staff at the time when he came to see me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And was that 8th July or when was it?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: At around that time, on the 8th approximately. Jankovic arrived as well as General Mladic. Jankovic accompanied Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, he's in the intelligence administration. You said he met you. What -- what did he say to you? What did you -- what kind of work did you do with him when he arrived on the 8th?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: He came to my office and told me that he was there on the orders of the Main Staff. He said that in the period during the operation, he was going to be with me in my office and that he was to take over all contact with the international organisations in Srebrenica, as well as all contact with DutchBat. In other words, he took over all the duties from within my remit of intelligence organ which had to do with the contact with organisations in Potocari and Srebrenica. He also said that in the ensuing period, he was to contact all of these organisations, including DutchBat. He told me he was there as ordered by the Main Staff of the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, when he was there in your office, sharing the office with you, was he sending reports on the situation up to the Main Staff, and were you -- it's a compound question, but were you also sending reports to your commander at the same time?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Colonel Jankovic sent reports, and we usually wrote them together in my office. Whenever we had information or any need to communicate with our superior command, when there were things we wanted to ask, we then drafted such reports together. I was familiar with their contents, and I knew that Colonel Jankovic was writing and submitting reports to his superior command. I also need to say here that I never drafted daily reports to my command -- for my command, but I did draft daily reports to my superior command, which was the department for security and intelligence at the command of the Drina Corps, and I continued doing so during the time Mr. Jankovic was in my office.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. And when Mr. Jankovic arrived, did you brief him as best you could on the security -- on the intelligence situation? Let me ask that again. Intelligence officer from the Main Staff comes down to the brigade. You're the intelligence officer in the brigade. Did you brief him about what was going on in your area of responsibility, the Bratunac Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I believe I can confirm that, but I think that Colonel Jankovic was from the intelligence administration, and he had everything I had had. All the information that had been sent to the Drina Corps, I am positive the same information was then passed on to the Main Staff. In other words, on the 8th, when Colonel Jankovic arrived, he had a clear picture of what was going on, and he was familiar with it. Of course, we discussed details of my contacts with DutchBat but nothing much more than that. I claim that Colonel Jankovic had all the information I had sent concerning the situation in Srebrenica. I need to say, for the sake of the Chamber, that I created an intelligence assessment which I forwarded to the corps command in the Main Staff which contained all the details about the situation in the enclave before the attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm sorry, I've lost track of how we do the schedule on these days. If we're stopping at noon, this would be a good time because I'm going to go into another chapter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Very well. We will take a break now --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- for half an hour. Shall we resume at -- before half past 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Nikolic, still talking about the period of the attack on Srebrenica enclave, up to -- from when it began to -- up through 11 July, did you learn in your capacity as security and intelligence officer whether or not civilian targets in the enclave -- or civilian objects or persons in the enclave had been targeted by the VRS during the attack?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes. With regard to this problem, I'm going to make a distinction between two things. First of all, we have artillery fire or mortar fire from the battalion on the town of Srebrenica, and I have my opinion, my own position, about this matter which I have expressed, and I want to express it again on this occasion. I don't know how the artillery was deployed exactly, and I cannot say anything precise about the dates on which the artillery was used, but as an intelligence officer from the brigade in which artillery was used against Srebrenica, what I know is that at the time of the operations, brigade artillery from the Bratunac Brigade was used, and fire was opened on the territory of the enclave. Fire was opened from 120-millimetre and 82-millimetre mortars. As far as the brigade's artillery is concerned, the Bratunac Brigade had 105-millimetre, 122- and 155-millimetre artillery pieces. The range of the artillery can reach Srebrenica. Srebrenica in the course of that operation was targeted by the artillery, and I want to be quite clear yet again. There were legitimate military targets in Srebrenica, commands, warehouses where equipment and weapons were kept and everything else, and these targets, these commands, regardless of the fact that they were in the town, were legitimate targets in my opinion. But given that there were a lot of people living in the core part of the town, I had information according to which during the shelling of the town of Srebrenica, a certain number of civilians were killed or seriously wounded. So I believe that opening fire in this way had as a result civilian casualties. Around the 11th, when a column of civilians, many civilians, were leaving Srebrenica in the direction of Potocari, I know that from positions of my 2nd Infantry Battalion that column of civilians was targeted. A B1 cannon targeted them. This is an artillery piece. It is a cannon, in fact, that fires directly at the targets in front of it. And when I asked why these civilians had been targeted, the 2nd Battalion responded by saying that they were observing from that observation post where the B1 was, and they thought that a lot of Muslim troops were moving from that direction, which is why they were targeted. So these are cases that I am familiar with, and I know that in such cases civilians were either killed or wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: So let me just make sure I'm clear on your answer talking about the B1 weapon that was part of the 2nd Battalion. Was that B1 -- 2nd Infantry Battalion. Was that B1 used to target the column moving from Potocari to Srebrenica [sic]?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes. In that particular case. The date is a specific one. The B1 cannon was firing on civilians who were moving from Srebrenica. They were almost at the entrance to Potocari, and this artillery piece opened fire on these civilians. From that position, there is a mount that is an elevation that is called Red Star and from that position you can see Potocari. It's as if Potocari were in the palm of your hand. So it is possible to use direct fire when targeting individuals.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I take it, Mr. Nicholls, that your question should have been reflected as column moving from Srebrenica to Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Correct. Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, let me move on and ask you some questions about the Hotel Fontana meetings on the 11th. Are you okay, Mr. Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, I'm fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you need at any time, please don't hesitate to -- to have a break.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm fine. I'm fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, the Trial Chamber has heard quite a lot of evidence about the meetings at Hotel Fontana on 11th July, so we won't go through everything to do with those meetings. I just want to know about where you were, what you saw, and what your role was. Now, did you hear about the first Hotel Fontana meeting on the 11th before it happened, and if so, how did you hear about it?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes. I heard that that meeting, the first one, was to be held on the 11th in the evening. I heard about that meeting. In fact, it was Colonel Jankovic who informed me about the fact that that meeting was to be held.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And then what did you do?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Colonel Jankovic told me that a meeting would be held, that General Mladic and DutchBat representatives would be present at that meeting. My task, which was a permanent one and that concerns all security organs, it concerned my own organ at the time, since the meeting was to be held in Fontana, I had to provide security for Fontana and prepare the premises where the meeting was to be held, which would be attended by the commander of the Main Staff, General Mladic. In addition, I was told that I was to send in the police and to provide an interpreter to help with the conversation between General Mladic and DutchBat representatives. I went with the commander of the military police, Mirko Jankovic, to Fontana. We provided a certain number of policemen and provided physical security for the Fontana building. We then emptied the entire Fontana building and none of the guests or soldiers remained in the building. We emptied the internal part and secured the premises where the meeting was to be held. Having made these preparations -- let me recap. My task was to act together with the commander of the military police and to provide security for the premises where the meeting was to be held and to provide security for the Fontana building as well. After we had done all of this, Colonel Jankovic arrived. He, myself and Mirko Jankovic -- or, rather, the interpreter, Petar Uscumlic, waited for General Mladic to arrive, as well as DutchBat members. They arrived, and, to be brief, the meeting took place in a small room in Hotel Fontana. I have to tell the Chamber that I wasn't present at the meeting. I was the officer whose duty was to provide security for the premises where the meeting was to be held. I was outside that small room, 3 or 4 metres away. I saw the participants in the meeting there. I saw what they were doing, how they were behaving. I could hear the subjects that they were discussing, because it was a small room, and an entire wall is like a harmonica that can be opened. Those doors were open. So we prepared the room in this manner before everyone arrived, and that's where the first meeting between General Mladic and the commander of the DutchBat, Mr. Karavaks was held.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Mr. Karremans.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. I understand, then, that you didn't participate in the meeting, but you observed the meeting from a few metres away; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And what did you do when the meeting had concluded? What happened next?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: After the meeting had ended, General Mladic said that the following meeting would be held that very same evening about 2200 hours or 2230 hours, and he said that security should be provided for the premises again. And the second meeting would again be held on the premises of the Fontana Hotel. Afterwards, I went to the Bratunac Brigade command, and that evening, on the 11th, I did what I had done on the previous days, on the days prior to the operation as well. I drafted a report on the situation and on the events that had taken place on that date, on the 11th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, the second meeting at approximately 2200 hours, or 10.00 p.m., did you provide security for that meeting as well? Just briefly tell us what you did there?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Everything I did for the first meeting, all the duties I performed with regard to organising the first meeting and securing the building and the individuals who participated at that meeting, well, I did exactly the same things when it came to organising the second meeting. That concerned the Fontana building, the interpreter, providing physical security, organising the arrival of General Mladic and the officers, the arrival of the Dutch and representatives of the Muslim side. I did everything that concerned or related to holding the meeting in the same building on the same premises. I had to make sure that the individuals participating in the meeting were safe when present in the building where the meeting was being held.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And again, did you observe the meeting from just outside but not participate in the meeting?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes. I can tell you who participated in the meeting. I think the Chamber already knows, but if necessary, I can give you their names. I wasn't a representative of the Serbian side participating in the discussions, so naturally it was Commander Ratko Mladic who spoke the most, who was the most important there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And just before we move on, securing the physical premises where a meeting is held with a member of the Main Staff, is that just a classical job of the security administration when there were visiting officers from senior command?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: As a rule, whenever there's a visit from the superior command, a visit by the corps commander or by his deputy, by someone from the Main Staff, in such cases the security organ takes all the necessary measures to provide security for individuals. The MPs' duties from -- have to provide security for the commanders or officers from the Main Staff. So that is a rule. These are legal provisions that have to be abided by, and as a chief of security, taking such measures would be part of the duties you have to perform.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, around the times of these meetings, did you receive information about the large column of persons in the enclave, large group of Muslims moving in a column from Srebrenica towards Potocari?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes. At that time in the evening hours, I had already received reports, mostly from the 2nd Infantry Battalion, from their positions, from their command, reports on the movement of a large number of civilians in the direction of the UNPROFOR base in Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And did you receive any information about the composition of that column of civilians? And what I'm getting at here is whether there were any men, able-bodied, military-aged men in that group of civilians.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: According to my assessments and the assessment of those subordinated to me in the 2nd Infantry Battalion and according to the general information that was passed down the chain of command and that I received through the professional line, according to all that information, in those columns there were, in our assessment - I'm speaking about our assessment - in that column there were between a thousand, 1.500 or 2.000 men who were fit for military service. But I must inform the Chamber of one thing which I think is important. We believed -- in fact, I make a distinction between men who were fit for military service and people who are militarily engaged within the 28th Division units. You can be fit for military service. You might be under an obligation to be mobilised into a unit, but that does not necessarily mean that you will be mobilised. So according to our assessment, since I roughly knew the number of people in the enclave, I roughly knew the structure of the population, how many women and children and men there were there, well, since that was the case, on the basis of previous assessments and previous information we believed that amongst those civilians there were between a thousand, 1.500 or 2.000 men fit for military service.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. So if I understood your answer, there were between 1.000, 1.500 or 2.000 men fit for military service but not necessarily that all of them were soldiers in the ABiH. Did I understand that correctly?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: That's quite correct. That's quite correct. That's what I wanted to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now when, the second Hotel Fontana meeting ended, can you tell us what you did afterwards? I'm now going to go chronologically through the events as you experienced them in the following days.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: After the second meeting, I received an order from the commander, from General Mladic, to escort the Dutch and the Muslim representatives to Potocari. Naturally, I carried out that order. I escorted them as far as the Yellow Bridge, which is at the border of the enclave, and then they continued from the Yellow Bridge to Potocari. And to tell you the truth, I did not enter Potocari that evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. One follow-up question. You said you knew the people at the meeting, and you just referred to the Muslim representative. Who -- if you remember, who was the Muslim representative at the second Hotel Fontana meeting, the one at night on the 11th of July.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes. I do remember that. The second meeting -- well, only at the second meeting was there a Muslim representative. Nesib Mandzic was his name. There was no Muslim representative at the first meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, after you returned from the Yellow Bridge, what did you do?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: After I returned from the Yellow Bridge, I think I went to the command. I think I wrote reports. I had contact with members of my brigade. I think I informed them about the situation. I referred them to information that related to the fall of the enclave, and I also mentioned the meetings and so on and so forth. I've already told you that there was oral information that was provided. I never wrote written reports for my command, but written reports on the entire situation and all the events, which included information on the movement of the Muslim civilians and our assessment of the composition of that group and the presence of men who were fit for military service, I provided all this information in written form to the Drina Corps and to the department for security and intelligence within that corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. And did you have any specific duty that night or were you -- did you do anything else after that? Or was that the end of the day on the 11th as far as your duties were concerned, when you finished your reports?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Well, I can't remember all the details right now, but mostly these activities concerned myself. There were probably certain other activities, but my activities mostly concerned my sector and my police. We performed these duties correctly, without any problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I was in the Bratunac Brigade command all that time, but I can't remember all the details precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That's fine. Thank you. So let's move on to the morning of 12 July. Now, first of all, early in the morning, around 8.00, was there a meeting at the Bratunac Brigade command, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: On the 12th, various meetings were held. I'm in a dilemma with regard to one of the meetings. I think the meeting was on the 13th at 8.00 in the morning, about 8.00 or half past 8.00 in the morning. On the 12th I was the duty officer, and I was in the operations room from 7.00, and I can't remember there was a meeting in the morning of the 12th. On the 13th, yes, but I can't remember a meeting on the 12th.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could I have P4373, please. I don't know if we can rotate that and blow it up in the Serbian language, please, so that ...

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Take a look at this document, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: As we saw recently, there were some issues with the English translation. I don't have a new translation yet, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: But I'll just ask, simply, Mr. Nikolic, if you could please read this document, which is a Zvornik CJB dispatch or report from 12 July 1995, from chief of CJB Dragomir Vasic, and it states in paragraph 2 -- it refers to a meeting at approximately 8.00 a.m. Can you read that document, or is it too -- is it illegible?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let us -- yes, that's what I meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's fine. At 8.00, in the area of the Bratunac Brigade, a meeting was held with Generals Mladic and Krstic at which tasks were issued to all the participants. Let me now see what it says. Yes. I remember this. It's difficult for me to list all of these meetings in chronological order in the command of my brigade, because there were so many official ones, and it's very difficult for me to remember all the meetings. But this meeting, I think I can actually remember it. It was held in the office, my commander's, above the operations room that I was in. This document has helped me refresh my memory.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, this document refers, in paragraph 5, to a meeting at 10.00 a.m. That's the third Hotel Fontana meeting. Once you read that I'm done with this document, and I'm going to ask you some questions about what happened next in the morning on 12 July.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes. I've read it. I've read it, and I know what it's about.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, were you given -- were you told about this 12 July meeting at Hotel Fontana in the morning and were you given tasks to secure the hotel again?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I apologise. With regard to the third meeting that was to be held on the 12th of July at 10.00 in the Fontana Hotel, I had information on the 11th in the evening. After the second meeting had been held I had information about that. It was then that General Mladic said -- or, rather, Mr. Karremans and General Mladic agreed that that meeting should be held the next day at 10.00 in the Fontana Hotel, and General Mladic and his team were supposed to attend the meeting. Mr. Karremans and his officers were to be present as well as Muslim representatives. And members of the Muslim army from Srebrenica were also to be present. So I knew that meeting was to be held on the 12th at 10.00 in the morning in Hotel Fontana. And when it comes to organisation, preparations, and providing security for the building and individuals, I had to do the very same things at that third meeting as the things that I did for the previous meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, in this third meeting on 12 July, where were you physically? Did you go into and observe the meeting or did you stay outside? What did you do during the meeting?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: At the time when the third meeting was held, I was not at Fontana. That is to say, I was not on the premises where the meeting was being held. For a while, that is to say, after I had taken care of the security and done everything else that was indispensable for having the meeting held, I sat at the reception desk for a while. So that is the first area that you see when you walk into the hotel. And for a while I was not even at the reception desk, but I was outside the hotel, in front of the hotel on this plateau where the police was, and basically I tried to make sure that all of this would evolve properly, because there was a great deal of interest. There were a lot of soldiers around Fontana, so I did not attend the meeting itself. I did not take part in it, and I did not hear the discussion that was held.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And you referred before to members of the Muslim army from Srebrenica were also to be present. In fact, did any representatives of the Muslim army, of the ABiH, attend this meeting? At least that's what we have in the transcript is: "And members of the Muslim army from Srebrenica were also to be present."

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I have already said that General Mladic insisted that this third meeting be attended by the representatives of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina -- or, rather, the 28th Division, in addition to the refugee population. However, apart from Mandzic -- and again, I don't know whether he was a soldier then, but I do know that he was engaged in the 28th Division. Then Nuhanovic, I was sure that he was not a soldier. And there was this woman who attended and she was not a soldier. Now, if Nuhanovic at the time was a soldier, then he was a representative of the army, and if not -- well, anyway, he introduced himself as a representative of the refugee population, a representative of the civilians, and that is how he introduced himself at the first two meetings. I heard that. He was quite explicit. He said that he could not represent the army, that he was not authorised to represent anyone from the military structures. That is what I heard from Nuhanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I am sorry. I apologise. Not Nuhanovic, Mandzic. Sorry, I see in the transcript that I said Nuhanovic, but actually I meant Mandzic, not Nuhanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Nesib Mandzic.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, Nesib. That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, I'm going to ask you about something else that you've talked about before. On 12 July 1995, in the morning, did you meet with any Drina Corps lieutenant-colonels that morning? Did you have a discussion with any officers from the Drina Corps that morning?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Before the meeting started, and it had been scheduled for 10.00, I saw two lieutenant-colonels and talked to them, Lieutenant-Colonel Popovic and Lieutenant-Colonel Kosoric. I mean, let me be quite clear straight away. This was no meeting, but it was a conversation that took place before they went to the meeting. So I talked to Lieutenant-Colonel Popovic, and I asked Lieutenant-Colonel Popovic what would happen next, and he said to me that there would be an operation of transferring Muslims, women and children, to free territory -- or, rather, Muslim-held territory and that military-aged men would be separated. Further on -- well, this is how the conversation evolved roughly. I asked him, Lieutenant-Colonel, sir, what would happen next, what are we going to do with the men who would be separated, and he said verbatim, in his very own way, that they should all be killed. I did not comment on that statement of his, what he said. And my first conclusion, I mean, my first thought was that in Potocari we would separate the military-aged men, that we would carry out this military triage. And that, quite simply, we would carry out a military task, that we would stick to military procedure, that we would single out those people from whom we had indicia or evidence or documents or witnesses to the effect that they had committed crimes, namely, that we would single them out and prosecute them. That was my first thought when I heard about the separation. After that, of course, you know what happened. When I arrived in Potocari, when the evacuation started, then it was absolutely clear to me what this was all about. I testified about that, and that was the first time that I had my doubts, and I think that that was the first time that it became clear to me that something bad was in the making for these people who had been singled out. I proposed -- or, rather, I suggested to him if we have people who have been separated, then -- I mean, if they are to be separated, then we have to ensure a place where they would be detained. So I thought that these men should be singled out, and there are certain buildings that are empty and where they could be kept. I told him that these were buildings in the centre of town, the elementary school Vuk Karadzic and buildings that are within that radius, about 100 metres. After that -- so, after that, in the presence of Mr. Kosoric as well, when he said that all the Muslims should be killed, we then had a discussion about two locations where these people should be killed. Ciglane and the Sase mine were mentioned. As far as the mine and the brick factory are concerned, these possible execution sites, I have to tell you one thing. I found out later, later, that is to say, after everything happened, before the men were separated, a certain number of officers went to the brick factory. They contacted the director, and they asked there about this place as a possible execution site. I don't know who these officers were. I don't have any names, and I don't know who they were. However, these are places that were mentioned as possible execution sites. As for the execution itself at these two locations, I want to say the following here: Neither at the brick factory or at Sase was a single one of these separated men killed, as far as I know. So there were no killings at any one of these two locations, Sase or the brick factory. After that -- so in front of that plateau, that is, there was yet another conversation. Kosoric was there, Petar Uscumlic and I. Also, we talked about the very same things, about evacuation, the arrival of the buses and so on, and roughly the position was the same. Everything that we had discussed with Popovic. Kosoric basically repeated the same thing to the same extent. While we were talking there, two Dutch officers came up. I think -- since I know them, I think it was Rave and another associate of his, and they asked me, "Mr. Nikolic, when will the bus arrive? When will this start?" And I said to them -- actually, I sent them to Acamovic, who was standing in front of Fontana, Colonel Acamovic, and I then I said to them that quite simply there was no need for them to wait there, to stay there, that they should go back to Potocari, that everything had been agreed upon, that everything had been taken care of, and that the evacuation would start. And that is what happened in front of the Fontana Hotel. The meeting -- or, rather, the conversation between myself and Popovic lasted five or seven minutes, ten minutes maximum. And then after that, he went to attend the meeting, he and Kosoric did, and I stayed in front of Fontana and worked on the security there, what my task was. That is more or less everything that was happening during those morning hours. And the conversation between myself, Mr. Kosoric, Popovic, Mr. Rave, and Uscumlic, Petar.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And when you say that Popovic and Kosoric then went to attend the meeting, is that the meeting in the Hotel Fontana?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's the meeting at the Fontana Hotel that was scheduled for 10.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, did you speak to Colonel Jankovic around this time? Did he give you any instructions about going yourself to Potocari?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: To the best of my recollection, I talked to Colonel Jankovic after the meeting. Once the Fontana meeting was over, Colonel Jankovic walked out of Fontana. I was standing on the plateau in front of Fontana and I was waiting for the end of the meeting with the police and the others who were providing security there at Fontana. And Colonel Jankovic walked out of Fontana and said that everything had been agreed upon about the transfer of Muslims to Kladanj, also that buses, trucks, fuel, everything, had been agreed upon, and Colonel Jankovic said to me that I should help during this evacuation -- or, rather, during this transfer of that population that was in Potocari. That is to say, transferring them to free territory under Muslim control. That was the area of Kladanj, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And did you ask Colonel Jankovic any questions about which units were going to take part in that operation in Potocari?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. I asked the colonel the following: "Colonel, sir, you know what the situation is in Potocari, you know how many people are there and how many things had to be done," and I asked who is going to do all of that. Colonel Jankovic said the following to me. He said that everything had been agreed upon, that commanders of the units that are in charge of this operation had already received orders and were issued with specific tasks, and that they were already in Potocari, from where the evacuation of these people was supposed to take place.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And did Colonel Jankovic instruct you to meet with anybody in particular when -- in Potocari? To contact anybody, put it that way.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes. He said to me that in Potocari, in addition to the army and the police, Dusko Jevic was there, who was in charge of part of the operation, and that I should talk to Dusko Jevic and help him, that I should meet up with him in Potocari, which I did, of course. And after the meeting was over and all of that, I got into my car and went to Potocari, because the only officer that I had contacted on that day, the 12th, was Dusko Jevic, nicknamed Stalin.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: What unit was Dusko Jevic an officer in?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Dusko Jevic was an officer in the special brigade of the MUP whose commander was General Saric, and the deputy commander was Ljubisa Borovcanin, and he was present there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Who was present there, Saric or Borovcanin? Present in Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Borovcanin was present, and he commanded the forces that were Special Police there.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the speaker's microphone please be adjusted. We have great trouble hearing him. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, would you speak into the microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, in addition to the Special Police, you've just described their being present, Mr. Borovcanin and Mr. Dusko Jevic, which other units, to the best that you remember, do you remember seeing in Potocari on the 12th of July? In other words, in addition to the Special Police, what other forces of the armed forces of Republika Srpska, either MUP or VRS, were present?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I will try to mention all of those I remember from Potocari. In addition to the unit of the special brigade of the MUP, part of the police forces, there was a unit that had dogs, German dogs. Then there were members of the station. Actually, policemen from the public security station in Bratunac. And there were members of a company. These were special purpose police units, and some of them were in Potocari. As for the military, there were parts of the military police from the Bratunac Brigade, that is to say, my own unit. Then there were members of the 2nd Infantry Battalion of the Bratunac Brigade. Then on the same day, a bit later, members of the 3rd Infantry Battalion of the Bratunac Brigade arrived. Then there were members of the Drina Wolves detachment. Their commander was Captain or Major Jolovic, Legenda. That's what he was called, or something like that. Then there were parts of the 65th Protection Regiment. That was a unit of the Main Staff, and parts of this unit were in Nova Kasaba. Then there were parts of the 10th Sabotage Detachment of the Main Staff. This was a unit of the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska. And there were parts of the battalion of the military police from the Drina Corps, that were part of the Drina Corps. I think I haven't forgotten anyone. These were units that were present, all of these that I have mentioned, that is to say, units of the 10th Sabotage Detachment. I mean, I knew them personally. Also, the units of the military police of the corps were involved in my own area, so I know them. I know these men from that police unit. And of course, from my brigade I knew everyone. So these were the units that were often engaged in the area of responsibility. These units were engaged in the operation of Srebrenica, and after Srebrenica fell, they were in Potocari. And in Potocari, in addition to all of these mentioned forces, there were also members of the Dutch Battalion at the spot where the evacuation of the civilian population was taking place after the third meeting on the 12th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. And if I understood your answer previously, Colonel Jankovic had told you before you arrived in Potocari that these units you saw there had already been given their orders.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes. Your understanding was correct. Yes, exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Going back a tiny bit, before the 11th of July and the 12th of July, did you see any members of Republika Srpska state security working in Bratunac, RDB operatives? And also, did you see any members of RDB state security in Potocari? If you can describe their presence during this time.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes. Let me just say for the benefit of the Trial Chamber, members of the state security, their centre was in Zvornik, and some of their operatives were in charge of the territory of the municipality of Bratunac as well. So the operative who worked permanently in the territory of Bratunac municipality was Sinisa Glogovac, if I remember his name correctly. And almost all the time he was in Bratunac. Actually, before the operation and during the operation, he was present. Then during the operation, actually after the fall of Srebrenica -- now, I don't know whether I'm going to remember the names. I think that in Bratunac -- no, it's not that I think. I saw him there. The boss of that centre was there, their chief. Mile is his name, I think, Mile Renovica. Then Sinisa, and I think that there was an operative from Zvornik, Vito. I think his last name was Tomic. And that would roughly be the team that was in charge there. Vito Glogovac and Sinisa were operatives, and Milanko Renovica was the chief of this centre. Now, was it a centre or whatever, but at any rate he was their boss. They were present before the fall of Srebrenica and they were present during -- well, before Srebrenica fell and they were present in Potocari. And together with the organ or organs that were in charge of separating the men, to the best of my knowledge, they worked on singling out these military-aged men, or, rather, those for whom they had had information to the effect that they had committed crimes during the previous operations. That would be it, roughly, as far as they are concerned. I also know two cases when they singled out a member of parliament at the time, Ibran Mustafa. Zlatan Celanovic assisted them in that. He knew Mustafic. And I also know a case about which I wrote a report to the command of the Drina Corps. A wounded man who they got out of the health centre there. The state security had singled him out, and he was suspected of having committed a crime. That Muslim was prosecuted and tried later, and I think that Ibran Mustafic, after the interviews, was transferred to Batkovici, I think. Both of them are alive to this day.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: We'll talk about that later, Ibran Mustafic. But was Mile the chief in Zvornik of the state security? I think you said his name was Mile Renovica; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. Mile Renovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, on the 12th of July, in addition to Ljubomir Borovcanin and Dusko Jevic, did you see any other -- can you tell us which officers you saw present from the Corps or the Main Staff, Drina Corps or the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I can tell you about all of those whom I saw in Potocari, but I think that there's no need. I mean, I can tell you in general terms, without any exception, all the officers from the Main Staff were in Bratunac, then came to Potocari on that day, the 12th, and they were all there. And all the officers from the command of the Drina Corps who were in Bratunac then on that day, the 12th, they all came to Potocari to see what it was that was happening. I think that there was not a single officer -- I mean, I don't want to say anything, but there was not a single officer from any command that was not present in Bratunac on that day and did not come to Potocari from Bratunac to see what was going on there. If you're interested in names, I'll give you all the names that I've already mentioned from the command of the Drina Corps, from the Main Staff, from my brigade, from the police. I can give you all the names.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Just for our record, I want it to be very clear, just give me the names of the Main Staff and Drina Corps officers you saw in Potocari on the 12th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: From the Main Staff, I know for sure I saw him, there was General Mladic and Colonel Jankovic. From the command of the Drina Corps, General Krstic was in Potocari, also General Zivanovic, Lieutenant-Colonel Popovic, Lieutenant-Colonel Kosoric, Colonel Acamovic, Lieutenant-Colonel Krsmanovic, and basically those are the persons I saw. Perhaps I may have forgotten someone. From the special brigade of the MUP there was Ljubisa Borovcanin, Dusko Jevic, I think -- no, I don't think. I'm sure. Mendeljev was there. I personally know him. He was commander of a company. From state security, from the RDB, there were those three men I mentioned, Sinisa Glogovac, Tomic, and Mile -- now, what was his last name, Mile's last name. Renovica, yes. Those were basically the officers basically there. And of course - I do apologise - from the Bratunac MUP there was a person who was often present. Miodrag Josipovic, chief of the MUP. And there was another officer. I cannot remember his name. He was from the public security station. At any rate, those are the officers that I remember from these different structures, that is to say, from the army, the regular police and the Special Police, and the state security.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Now, you told us before you went to Potocari you had an idea -- early in the day you had an idea of what would happen with the men there and how they would be treated. Tell us what you saw, in your own words, in Potocari about what happened to the population there. What happened to the women and children, what happened to the men?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: When the buses and trucks arrived, then people started being put onto them. In the first convoy, as far as I could see, in addition to women and children, there was a number of men who were released as well. There was some problem with the convoy movement and the buses, et cetera, and as I was local, I told Dusko Jevic to move some 300 metres up the road to where there was a parking place, and that's where the evacuation started. As I've said, on the first convoy there were some men plus the women and children. The first convoy was escorted by members of DutchBat. They were in their vehicles. I learned from Colonel Jankovic that the arrangement was such that the convoys be escorted by DutchBat soldiers. After that, the separation of men began. All the men who were in Potocari moving towards the buses were singled out at a certain point and separated from the women and children. When I was there, throughout my stay there, the following happened: Men were being separated, and during the separation they were mistreated. First of all, all their belongings were taken away, such as bags, and all that was thrown onto a pile. Next, they took away their rings, bracelets, necklaces, anything else that the people had on them. The items were taken away by the soldiers who were carrying out the separation. They were then put into a number of houses nearby that were used for temporary detention. They also kicked them and hit them. They hit them with rifle butts and all such things that were quite unbelievable. All this is something I could observe. It was a very difficult, horrible situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And how did you react personally?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: How did you react personally? Did you try to stop this mistreatment, these beatings, this taking of property?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I could see it all. As a human being, I could have stood up to everything that was going on. As a soldier, as an officer, and a member of the Bratunac Brigade, I neither had the might, nor did I have any command authority or a unit that could stop them from doing so. Simply put, I did not try, and I did not dare either to help the soldiers or to stop them. God forbid if anything like that should happen again, irrespective of everything, I would try to help such people. I didn't then, because as I have testified already, because in 1992, I had had a bad experience when I stood up to the then authorities, following which I was assaulted, physically mistreated and hospitalised. I was away for four to five months because of the attack. And the people who caused it all were from the 10th Sabotage Detachment, the 65th Protection Regiment and all those over whom no one could really have control, or power, discipline. That is why I simply did not dare order any assistance to the detainees. I did assist certain individuals, and they are still alive. They even got in touch once I was in The Hague. I also saved whole families and put the them on the buses, but these were individual instances. I didn't do anything generally to help the people. I helped those I knew. They live and are still in contact, but I don't think it was enough to help.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls, we need to adjourn for today. Yes. We will resume tomorrow at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 14th day of February, 2012, at 9.00 a.m.
